title: Khanates of the Caucasus
capsule: The Khanates of the Caucasus were a collection of semi-autonomous Persianate principalities that emerged in the South Caucasus and adjacent territories from the 1740s as Safavid authority collapsed, each ruled by a khan of Iranian Turkic or local origin nominally subordinate first to Nadir Shah and then to the Zand and Qajar dynasties of Iran. The principal khanates included Karabakh, Shirvan, Shaki, Baku, Quba, Ganja, Nakhchivan, Erivan, and Talish, spanning the territory of modern Azerbaijan, Armenia, and parts of Georgia. Russian expansion under Catherine II and Alexander I progressively absorbed them: the Gulistan Treaty (1813) and Turkmenchay Treaty (1828) transferred most remaining khanates to Russia, ending the period of de facto autonomous Caucasian khans.
attestation: Boundaries from Seshat Cliopatria (Bennett et al., Scientific Data 2025; CC BY 4.0), digitized from standard historical atlases at ~0.07° resolution. The Khanates of the Caucasus represents an aggregate of distinct polities with varying boundaries; individual khanate territories are partially attested through Russian colonial surveys, but boundary data before Russian conquest is limited.
